title: Where is thy sting?
hookLine: Paul: O death, where is thy sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55)

lines: PAUL TURNS AND SPEAKS TO DEATH.
cards: A letter is being read aloud to the church in Corinth. The writer is Paul, and he has heard something troubling: some there say there's no rising from the dead at all.
His question is blunt: "how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?" A long, careful argument follows. Then, near the end, it stops sounding like an argument.
Paul turns from the people in the room and speaks straight to death, the way you'd speak to a bully who has finally been cornered.

teach.b: Paul doesn't pretend death is gentle or natural or fine. He calls it by its name: "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." Whatever comfort comes next doesn't start by shrinking the loss.
To explain how the dead could rise, he reaches for a farmer's picture: "that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die."

teach.h: A SEED SOWN, A BODY RAISED.
teach.b: A seed goes into the ground, and what comes up looks nothing like the seed. "It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption." The body that rises, in Paul's telling, is changed, not just restarted.
When that change comes, he says, "then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory." Some readers trace that saying to the prophets Isaiah and Hosea.
Then the taunt: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" It's almost playful, a little mocking, the tone of someone sure of how the story ends.
And he names the sting: "The sting of death is sin," and then, "thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ."
For Christians, the line doesn't deny that people die or that grief hurts; Paul has just called death an enemy.
It's a claim about who wins in the end: a sting and a victory, both asked after as if they had gone missing.

how: Some churches read 1 Corinthians 15 at funerals and at Easter, and the words "O death, where is thy sting?" are read aloud or sung in services about the resurrection.

o: the disciple who denied Jesus three times in one night
a prophet who wrote that death is a gentle friend
the apostle who wrote to Corinth that death will not win

games.q: what's inside Paul's chapter — tap the pairs.

s: in this chapter Paul calls death a friend
he calls it the last enemy that shall be destroyed.
Paul was answering people who said there is no resurrection
"how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?"
Paul says the line fulfills a saying that is written
"then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written."

games.q: you're Paul. people in a church you know well say no one rises from the dead. how does your argument end?
o: by agreeing to drop the subject.
by turning and speaking straight to death: where is thy sting?
by telling them death doesn't hurt.
games.why: after calling death an enemy, Paul taunts it: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?

practice: Let the line go by with your breath, one piece on each out-breath: O death, where is thy sting, O grave, where is thy victory. Then notice what comes, defiance, doubt, comfort or nothing at all, without deciding what it should be.
If you pray, you can let Paul's thanks follow the questions.

wordCard.voice: Paul, who taunts death in his letter to the Corinthians, claiming death is swallowed up in victory and will not win in the end. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: swallowed up in victory. For Paul, the enemy is real, and it loses. Day seven hundred seventy-eight, done.
